cards.title: Welcome Email Series with Unique Per-Subscriber Coupon Codes
cards.summary: Build a multi-email welcome automation where each subscriber receives a personally generated single-use discount code.
cards.use_when: You are setting up the opt-in to first-purchase email flow and want a personal, trackable discount instead of one shared public code.
steps: Create the opt-in form on the site (name + email) and connect it to an email platform automation workflow.
In the workflow builder, add an email step and insert the 'unique discount code' element so the platform generates a one-code-per-contact coupon, not a static code.
Set the coupon expiry once in the workflow settings; it is calculated automatically per recipient, so you should NOT adjust the expiry date per individual email.
Personalize the copy with the subscriber's first name, and include a redeemable copy button plus a link that applies the code at cart/checkout.
Add a second email with a different angle or urgency, then a third, so the sequence continues beyond the first message (e.g., day 1, then day 4).
Remove any leftover block or element not needed in the follow-up emails before publishing.
Publish and finish the workflow, then test the full path: sign up with a real or test email, receive the code, add a product, apply the coupon at cart, and check out.
Verify in the store's coupon list that a unique coupon was created and is restricted to a single use for that contact.
caveats: The unique discount code feature is platform-specific; verify the current element name and location in your email tool's interface.
Confirm that coupon usage limits and expiry are actually enforced by your store coupon settings after the code is generated.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Split Testing Email Subject Lines and Content to Lift Revenue
cards.summary: Use drag-and-drop A/B split testing on emails to find subject lines and content that increase opens and sales.
cards.use_when: You have an established email flow or campaign and want to improve open rates or revenue per send.
steps: In your email platform's workflow or campaign builder, locate the split/A-B testing element and drag it into the flow.
Duplicate the email into two branches and change one variable at a time, e.g., change only the subject line to 'last chance' vs. the original.
Assign a portion of the list to each variant so results are comparable rather than sending different messages sequentially.
Publish and let the test run long enough to collect meaningful data before declaring a winner (two-day tests are too short for strong conclusions).
Compare open rate first, then clicks and sales, and keep the winning version as the standard for that send.
Repeat tests on other emails in the sequence so improvements accumulate across the whole flow.
caveats: The presenter claims A/B testing can 'increase revenue big time' — treat that as a general argument for testing, not a guaranteed result.
Short tests (e.g., a day) give unreliable winners; avoid acting on tiny sample sizes.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Abandoned Cart Email Triggered by Cart Inactivity
cards.summary: Set up an automation that emails shoppers who add an item to cart but do not purchase within a defined inactivity window.
cards.use_when: You want to recover checkout/cart abandonment without manual outreach.
steps: Create a new workflow in your email platform and select the abandoned cart trigger.
Set the trigger to fire on cart inactivity after a realistic window (the tutorial uses one hour in production; one minute was used only for demo purposes).
Build the email with a subject line that creates urgency (e.g., 'items in your cart are selling out fast').
Dynamically insert the actual cart contents so the recipient sees the specific product(s) and a link back to buy.
Activate the workflow so it runs automatically as soon as shoppers opt in and leave items in the cart.
Test end-to-end: add a product, stop activity, confirm the email arrives and the product link resolves correctly.
caveats: The one-minute delay was only for demonstration — production delays should reflect real shopping behavior, typically at least one hour.
This flow depends on the visitor being identifiable (e.g., opted in or logged in) for the email address to be captured.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Behavioral and Value-Based Subscriber Segments Feeding Targeted Automations
cards.summary: Create segments from email engagement, purchase behavior, region, and value, then trigger tailored workflows when contacts enter a segment.
cards.use_when: You want to send different offers to different customer groups automatically rather than one list-wide campaign.
steps: Go to the audience segments area and use AI creation or the pre-built segment templates to define groups.

Build segments such as: active email subscribers, birthdays, inactive subscribers (no opens or purchases across recent weeks/months or last ~20 emails), geographically grouped (e.g., Europe), recent buyers, and high-value subscribers (active openers who purchase).
Create a new workflow from scratch and select 'entered a segment' as the trigger, then choose the specific segment.
Add an appropriate delay (e.g., 10 days for a high-value segment) before sending.
Send a segment-specific message, e.g., a 15% extra discount for three days to customers who spent over $1,000, or a 'we miss you' offer (e.g., 50% off for two days) to inactive subscribers.
Activate each workflow so offers fire automatically as contacts qualify for or move between segments.
Review segment membership periodically to ensure the criteria still match your intent.
caveats: The 'bought more than $1,000' and discount levels (15%, 50%) are illustrative examples from the tutorial, not recommended thresholds.
Confirm the actual segment criteria options in your email platform's interface before building, as names and logic may change.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Custom Branded Order Confirmation Email Replacing the Default
cards.summary: Create a styled order confirmation workflow so customers receive a better-looking confirmation than the default store email.
cards.use_when: Your default WooCommerce order confirmation looks generic and you want a branded post-purchase touchpoint.
steps: In your email platform, create a new workflow and select the order confirmation trigger (search 'confirmation' if needed).
Edit the email content and maintain consistent styling, including button settings (e.g., primary button color/style) to match your brand.
Finish editing and start the workflow.
Test by placing a real or test order through checkout, and confirm that the customer receives the branded email (you as the shop owner will still see the WooCommerce order notification).
Decide whether to use the platform's version instead of the default store confirmation going forward.
caveats: The default WooCommerce confirmation still fires by default; manage messaging to avoid customers receiving confusing duplicates if both are active.
Verify current trigger names and settings in the email platform, as interfaces change.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Revenue Attribution: Separating Platform-Driven Sales from Total Store Revenue
cards.summary: Use your email/automation platform's tracking to see how much revenue is directly driven by automations versus the store as a whole.
cards.use_when: You want to judge whether your email automations and opt-in offers are actually driving revenue before investing further.
steps: Connect your email platform to your store so it can track sales originating from its automations (the tutorial shows the platform distinguishing WooCommerce-driven vs. platform-driven sales).
In the platform dashboard, compare total store revenue against the revenue attributed to automations.
Use campaign-level reporting to see how many sales came from a specific broadcast to the whole list.
Use this split to decide where to invest: more automation, better flows, or list-building campaigns.
Re-measure after each significant change to see whether attributed revenue moves.
caveats: Attribution logic is platform-dependent and can overlap; treat platform-attributed revenue as directional, not exact.
The tutorial's figures ($1,991 total, $900 from automations) are one example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Swap Shared Discount Codes for Unique, Single-Use, Time-Limited Codes
cards.summary: Use per-contact, expiry-limited, single-use coupon codes so discounts can be tracked to individuals and cannot be reused.
cards.use_when: You are designing an opt-in incentive and want protection against code sharing and clearer attribution.
steps: Use an automation element that generates a unique coupon code per subscriber rather than publishing one universal discount code.
Set an expiry window (the tutorial used seven days) so urgency is created and liability is limited.
Enforce single use so the code cannot be redeemed again once used.
Confirm in your store's coupon list that the code appears, is limited to one use, and carries the intended expiry date.
Deliver the code so the shopper can copy it and apply it at cart.
Test applying the code yourself, then verify that it is marked used and cannot be reused.
caveats: Confirm your store's coupon settings actually enforce single-use and expiry after the platform generates the code.
Manage the operational burden of many coupon records as your list grows.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Editing Homepage Content, Product Blocks and Prices in the Site Editor
cards.summary: Directly edit homepage text, images, product references, prices and styling in the WordPress block editor by clicking and adjusting right-side settings.
cards.use_when: You need to update your store homepage hero, featured product blocks, or promotional text without a developer.
steps: Open the page for editing and triple-click (or click into) a text block to change copy directly.

For a button: open the style tab to set hover behavior (e.g., darken or scale) and the borders/shadows settings to adjust border radius; in the details panel, set the link and type the target product/page name so the editor auto-suggests matching products, pages and posts.
For a featured product image: select the image block, choose select image, and replace it with the product photo.
Update the price text manually to the new value (e.g., $90.99); if the text is too large, adjust size under typography.
Repeat for a second featured product block the same way.
For icons, click the icon block and search for a replacement icon.
Dynamic sections like 'Arrivals' are auto-fetched from the store, so verify they reflect the intended products rather than editing them by hand.
For background images: open style > background and choose a new image; for text color, open style > typography and set the color (e.g., white) per text block.
To add new page areas, click and add a block (or type '/' to pick a block type).
caveats: Manually edited prices can drift out of sync with actual product prices — update both when you change pricing.
Exact block names and panels vary by theme/editor version; verify against your current WordPress editor.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Making the Header, Menu and Off-Canvas Mobile View Responsive
cards.summary: Use the editor's tablet/mobile preview to fix header, menu, logo and icon styling so the site works on all devices.
cards.use_when: Your site looks broken on tablet or mobile and you need to correct layout and styling for smaller screens.
steps: Open the header/footer builder and switch to the tablet/mobile view.
Check how elements render on the smaller breakpoint and identify what looks wrong or misaligned.
In the design settings, set the background (e.g., light), swap the logo for the appropriate version, and confirm it updates.
Select the main menu, go to design, set text color (e.g., dark) and the hover color (e.g., orange); adjust fonts as needed.
Add or adjust the location/HTML block with matching dark-text and orange-hover styling.
Switch to mobile view, open the off-canvas menu area, and under design set the icon color (e.g., dark) so the X/close control is visible.
Publish and re-check both tablet and mobile to confirm the header, menu and off-canvas behavior are correct.
caveats: The specific settings paths depend on your builder/theme; verify the current options in your editor.
Always preview on desktop, tablet and mobile after changes before publishing.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Optional Channels: Texts and Push Notifications Alongside Email
cards.summary: Extend your automation workflows to SMS and push notifications when you have the subscriber's contact details.
cards.use_when: Your list includes phone numbers or app/device access and you want to reach people beyond the inbox.
steps: If you collect phone numbers, add an SMS step in the workflow (additional to the email steps).
If push notifications are available, add a push step so subscribers see the message on their device.
Use timing/delay controls so channels do not fire simultaneously and overwhelm the contact.
Use tags for context so a step only sends when a contact has a specific tag (e.g., only send this offer to a particular group).
Test each channel separately to confirm delivery before activating.
caveats: SMS requires collecting phone numbers and appropriate consent; only send where you have permission.
Channel availability depends on your platform and integrations — verify current support.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Using Tags to Conditionally Gate Automation Emails
cards.summary: Apply tags to contacts and use them as conditions so emails only send to appropriately grouped people.
cards.use_when: You want certain workflow emails to fire only for a subsection of subscribers (e.g., a specific offer or cohort).
steps: Assign meaningful tags to contacts based on behavior or source (e.g., a tag identifying a specific interest or purchase context).
In the workflow, add a condition/tag step that checks whether the contact has the required tag.
Place the conditional email after the tag check so only tagged contacts proceed.
Use delays before or after the tag condition to control timing.
Test with a tagged and an untagged contact to confirm the email only reaches the intended group.
caveats: Tag hygiene matters — a bloated or inconsistent tag scheme causes misfires.
Conditional logic naming and placement differ by platform; verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx

cards.title: Prioritizing Your Next Store Improvements: SEO and Email First
cards.summary: The presenter ranks learning SEO (via a rank-tracking plugin) and email marketing as the highest-value follow-on skills for a WooCommerce store.
cards.use_when: You have a functioning store and are deciding which growth skill or project to invest in next.
steps: If your store lacks organic discovery, prioritize learning search optimization and using a rank-tracking plugin to be found in search results.
If you already have traffic but weak repeat revenue, prioritize deepening your email list and automation setup.
Treat affiliate marketing as an optional, separate monetization path (promoting other people's products) rather than a core store requirement.
Pick one priority at a time and implement it fully before moving on.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated opinion on prioritization, not a proven universal rule; your store's bottleneck should drive the choice.
The presenter's affiliate earnings figure is a personal example, not a promise of results.
cards.source_name: How To Start an Online Store That Runs on Autopilot (WooCommerce Tutorial).docx
